questions.prompt: What do two descriptors produced by dup share?
options: Two independent file offsets
One open-file description, including its offset and status flags
A copy of the inode's data blocks
The directory entry and nothing else
questions.explanation: dup installs another fd-table entry that refers to the same open-file description. A later read or lseek on either descriptor moves that one offset.

questions.prompt: Why is the user-facing handle an integer rather than a kernel address?
options: Integers are faster than pointers on every CPU
User code must not forge or dereference a kernel object
The integer itself stores the file bytes
The page cache requires the handle to be smaller than a page
questions.explanation: The kernel maps the integer through the process fd table. Handing out a kernel pointer would expose an address the process must not be able to invent or follow.

questions.prompt: Where does a second open of the same path start, with no O_APPEND?
options: At the first descriptor's current offset
At a new open-file description positioned at the start for an ordinary read
At EOF, always
Inside the other process's fd table
questions.explanation: open allocates a new open-file description. The lab's second read returns the leading bytes while the dup'd pair continues from the shared offset.

questions.prompt: What does closing one of two dup'd descriptors do?
options: Destroys the open-file description immediately
Drops one reference and leaves the description while another descriptor still names it
Rewinds the shared offset to zero
Creates a new inode
questions.explanation: Each descriptor is a reference. The description, including its offset, remains until the last reference is closed.

days.title: Short Reads, Writes, and Nonblocking I/O

questions.prompt: A write returns a positive count smaller than the request. What is that?
options: Failure, with no bytes transferred
A short success; the caller continues from the bytes already transferred
Proof the file offset did not move
A request the kernel will finish without further calls
questions.explanation: A positive return is the count transferred. The lab's nonblocking pipe write of more than the pipe capacity returns a short count and the retry loop continues.

questions.prompt: How does read returning 0 differ from EAGAIN on a pipe?
options: They are the same outcome
0 means no write ends remain; EAGAIN means this nonblocking call found no bytes yet
EAGAIN means every writer has closed
0 means the caller's buffer was shorter than PIPE_BUF
questions.explanation: EOF is a zero return after the writers are gone. EAGAIN is the nonblocking empty-pipe result while a writer can still produce bytes.

questions.prompt: What does EINTR from read mean when the handler was installed without SA_RESTART?
options: The descriptor is closed
A signal interrupted the wait; retry if the transfer is still wanted
The bytes that were requested are corrupt
The call must not be issued again
questions.explanation: The lab blocks in read, delivers SIGUSR1, and observes EINTR. The robust loop treats that return as 'try again', not as EOF or as a short success.

questions.prompt: What does O_NONBLOCK change about an empty pipe read?
options: It makes short writes impossible
The call returns EAGAIN instead of sleeping the task
It disables signals
It enlarges the pipe to PIPE_BUF
questions.explanation: Nonblocking mode is how the lab makes EAGAIN deterministic. The task stays runnable and the caller decides whether to wait another way.

days.title: VFS, the Page Cache, and Durability

questions.prompt: A second open reads a write that has not been fsync'd. What did the lab observe?
options: Crash durability
Same-machine visibility through the page cache
A device write barrier
A sparse hole
questions.explanation: Buffered write updates cache pages. A later read on this machine can see those bytes before any durability request. That visibility is not survival across power loss.

questions.prompt: What does a successful fsync establish in this lab?
options: The bytes will survive every power loss
The kernel accepted a durability request, which is not a crash-proof claim
The page cache dropped the pages
stat will fail afterwards
questions.explanation: fsync asks the kernel to push data toward stable storage. Drive caches, filesystem behavior, and power loss sit outside what this userspace result proves.

questions.prompt: Which trio matches the sparse-file run?
options: Logical size equal to the allocated byte count, and no zero byte
Logical size past the hole, a zero byte in the hole, and fewer allocated blocks than that size
st_size zero after the tail write
Two descriptors sharing one offset
questions.explanation: The logical end is the tail write. A read in the gap returns zero. st_blocks, in 512-byte units, stays far below the logical size when the filesystem records a hole.

questions.prompt: What does the VFS normalize for this week?
options: CPU page-table permissions
One read/write/stat interface over different kernel objects
The numeric value of PIPE_BUF
C memory ordering
questions.explanation: Regular files, pipes, and other objects are reached through a file object and its operations. The page cache is the file-page layer under that interface, not the pipe buffer and not the page tables.

questions.prompt: When does a pipe read return 0?
options: As soon as any one write-end descriptor is closed
When every write end is closed and the buffered bytes are gone
Whenever the read end is nonblocking
After exactly PIPE_BUF bytes have been written
questions.explanation: The lab closes one dup'd writer and still sees EAGAIN. The zero return appears only after the last writer closes.

questions.prompt: What does dup2 of a pipe write end onto STDOUT_FILENO do in the child?
options: Copies the bytes into a second pipe
Makes standard output refer to that pipe's open-file description
Changes the parent's standard output
Sets O_APPEND on the read end
questions.explanation: dup2 is another fd-table slot for the same description. The child writes redir-ok to fd 1 and the parent reads it from the pipe.

questions.prompt: A nonblocking write on a full pipe returns EAGAIN. What is that?
options: Silent data loss
Backpressure: the pipe cannot accept more bytes until a reader drains it
End of file
An atomic partial write of PIPE_BUF
questions.explanation: The finite pipe buffer is the flow-control point. O_NONBLOCK turns the would-block sleep into EAGAIN so the producer stays bounded.

questions.prompt: A nonblocking write of at most PIPE_BUF bytes finds too little free space. What does POSIX require?
options: A short prefix is written
The call fails with EAGAIN and transfers nothing
The call blocks despite O_NONBLOCK
The reader observes a torn mix of that write
questions.explanation: Writes of PIPE_BUF bytes or fewer are atomic. On a full pipe the lab's nonblocking PIPE_BUF write returns EAGAIN; on an empty pipe the same size write completes.

questions.prompt: What do select, poll, and epoll provide that one blocking read does not?
options: A copy of the bytes into the page cache
A way for one task to sleep until any of several descriptors can make progress
Atomicity up to PIPE_BUF
Crash durability
questions.explanation: Readiness is a scheduling facility. The task leaves the CPU until a descriptor can accept or produce progress, instead of blocking inside a single read or spinning.

questions.prompt: After a level-triggered epoll report, a one-byte read leaves bytes queued. The next wait with timeout zero should:
options: Stay silent until another write
Report readiness again because the level is still true
Convert the pipe to blocking mode
Close the writer
questions.explanation: Level-triggered notification tracks the current condition. The lab sees epoll_lt_partial=ready after the partial read.

questions.prompt: What must an edge-triggered reader do with bytes left after the notification?
options: Wait for epoll to repeat the same edge
Drain until EAGAIN, because the same edge is not repeated
Assume the next read will return 0
Clear O_NONBLOCK before the next wait
questions.explanation: The lab's ET wait after a partial read returns not-ready. The remaining bytes are still there and are consumed by reading until EAGAIN. A later write is a new edge.

questions.prompt: select reports readable, then read returns fewer bytes than requested. Why is that coherent?
options: select failed
Readiness means a call can make progress, not that the whole request is buffered
dup split the pipe into two buffers
EINTR always shortens a ready read
questions.explanation: The lab asks for 100 bytes, four are queued, and read returns 4. Ready is not a full-transfer contract.

days.title: mmap, Shared Mappings, and Data Movement

questions.prompt: A MAP_SHARED store is visible to pread before msync. What does that show?
options: A completed disk write barrier
The mapping and the file read share the same cached pages
MAP_PRIVATE copy-on-write
That mmap is faster than read on every machine
questions.explanation: MAP_SHARED updates the file's pages. pread observes those bytes through the page cache. Visibility here is still not crash durability.

questions.prompt: How should this lab's msync(MS_SYNC) be described?
options: Proof the bytes survive power loss
A request to write mapped modifications back, not a crash-proof result
A substitute for munmap
A prerequisite before any pread can see a MAP_SHARED store
questions.explanation: The store was already visible before msync. msync completion means the request returned, which this module does not promote into a crash-durability claim.

questions.prompt: What can one timed pread versus one memcpy from the mapping establish?
options: mmap is universally faster
A single-run observation for this size, machine, and cache state
Block-layer service time
The TLB cost on every architecture
questions.explanation: The lab prints both durations and performance_claim=none. Order can change with size, faults, cache warmth, and filesystem.

questions.prompt: A later pwrite shows up inside the MAP_SHARED mapping. That is evidence of:
options: An accidental MAP_PRIVATE mapping
Coherence between write and the shared mapping on this Linux behavior
msync failure
A sparse hole at offset zero
questions.explanation: The lab checks the bytes at offset 32 in the mapping after pwrite. MAP_SHARED is the mode that makes that comparison meaningful.

days.title: I/O Debugging and a Comparison Report

questions.prompt: What is /proc/self/fd/N evidence of?
options: A second stored copy of the file bytes
The process fd table, via a symlink to the object that descriptor names
The page-cache offset
The numeric PIPE_BUF
questions.explanation: readlink and the directory listing identify which integer is open and which path it names. They do not duplicate the file's data.

questions.prompt: What does read return on a descriptor this process has already closed?
options: 0, meaning EOF
EBADF
EAGAIN
EPIPE
questions.explanation: EBADF means that integer is not an open descriptor in this process. EOF would mean a still-open object has no more bytes.

questions.prompt: With SIGPIPE ignored, a write to a pipe whose read end is closed returns:
options: EPIPE
EBADF
A short positive count
questions.explanation: No reader remains, so the write fails with EPIPE. Ignoring SIGPIPE lets the process observe that errno instead of dying.

questions.prompt: epoll_ctl on a regular file returns EPERM here. What belongs in the report?
options: A claim that epoll is missing from the kernel
The operation, the descriptor kind, and the errno, without a broader guess
A claim that the page cache rejected the call
A requirement to switch that file to edge trigger
questions.explanation: EPERM is the Linux result for an fd that does not support epoll. A closed fd and a closed epoll instance are separate EBADF results. Record each one.
